claims.source: CRISPR-mediated loss-of-function mutations in Lss, required for an early step in the pathway, and in Dhcr7 and Dhcr24, required for the terminal steps, impaired the transcriptional induction of endogenous Gli1 (an immediate target gene used as a measure of signaling strength) (Figure 2B and C; CRISPR-edited alleles shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claims.claim: The abundance of cholesterol was reduced in Dhcr7-/- and Dhcr24-/- cells.
claims.source: Quantitative mass spectrometry measurements and intact cell staining with a cholesterol-binding probe confirmed that the abundance of cholesterol was reduced in Dhcr7-/- and Dhcr24-/- cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and probe staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: The abundances of 7-dehydrocholesterol and desmosterol were elevated in Dhcr7-/- and Dhcr24-/- cells, respectively.
claims.source: Conversely, the abundances of substrates for Dhcr7 and Dhcr24, 7-dehydrocholesterol and desmosterol, respectively, were elevated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E.

claims.claim: HH signaling in Lss-/- cells could be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol.
claims.source: HH signaling in both Lss-/- and Dhcr7-/- cells, but not in Dhcr24-/- cells, could be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol, pointing to cholesterol deficiency as the cause of impaired HH signaling (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claims.claim: HH signaling in Dhcr7-/- cells could be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol.
claims.source: HH signaling in both Lss-/- and Dhcr7-/- cells, but not in Dhcr24-/- cells, could be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol, pointing to cholesterol deficiency as the cause of impaired HH signaling (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claims.claim: HH signaling in Dhcr24-/- cells could not be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol.
claims.source: HH signaling in both Lss-/- and Dhcr7-/- cells, but not in Dhcr24-/- cells, could be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol, pointing to cholesterol deficiency as the cause of impaired HH signaling (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claims.claim: Rescue of HH signaling defects in Dhcr7-/- cells by exogenous cholesterol has been demonstrated previously.
claims.source: Rescue of HH signaling defects in Dhcr7-/- cells by exogenous cholesterol has also been demonstrated previously (Blassberg et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: DHCR24 is the only enzyme that is required for cholesterol biosynthesis but dispensable for 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol synthesis.
claims.source: 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol is a unique oxysterol that is not synthesized from cholesterol but rather made through a shunt pathway that closely parallels the post-squalene cholesterol biosynthesis pathway (Figure 2A). Exogenously added 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol can bind and activate SMO, so it has been proposed that this oxysterol (present at ~1% of the levels of cholesterol in cells) may be an endogenous SMO agonist regulated by PTCH1 (Qi et al., 2019b; Raleigh et al., 2018). Interestingly, DHCR24 is only used in the Kandutsch-Russell and Bloch pathways for cholesterol synthesis but not in the shunt pathway for the synthesis of 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol (Sharpe and Brown, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and the pathway diagram in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Loss of DHCR24 blocks HH signaling without reducing 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol abundance.
claims.source: The fact that loss of DHCR24 blocks HH signaling (Figure 2A and C) without reducing 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol abundance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) suggests that cholesterol rather than 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol regulates HH signaling.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Cholesterol itself, rather than a precursor or a metabolite, is the endogenous sterol lipid that regulates SMO activation.
claims.source: In summary, the data from our genetic screen support the view that cholesterol itself, rather than a precursor or a metabolite, is the endogenous sterol lipid that regulates SMO activation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic screen results.

claims.claim: Sptlc2 is the first committed step in sphingolipid synthesis from L-serine and palmitoyl-CoA.
claims.source: Top hits from this screen include Sptlc2, the first committed step in sphingolipid synthesis from L-serine and palmitoyl-CoA, as well as Sgms1, which converts ceramide to sphingomyelin (SM).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of sphingolipid biosynthesis.

claims.claim: Sgms1 converts ceramide to sphingomyelin (SM).
claims.source: Top hits from this screen include Sptlc2, the first committed step in sphingolipid synthesis from L-serine and palmitoyl-CoA, as well as Sgms1, which converts ceramide to sphingomyelin (SM).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of sphingolipid biosynthesis.

claims.claim: The identification of Sgms1 suggests that SM is the relevant product of the sphingolipid pathway that attenuates HH signaling.
claims.source: The identification of Sgms1 suggests that SM is the relevant product of the sphingolipid pathway that attenuates HH signaling.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the screen results.

claims.claim: Myriocin is a fungal antibiotic that inhibits SPTLC2.
claims.source: Myriocin is a fungal antibiotic that inhibits SPTLC2 (Figure 3A) and is commonly used to deplete SM in cells (Courtney et al., 2018; Tafesse et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and established knowledge.

claims.claim: Myriocin is commonly used to deplete SM in cells.
claims.source: Myriocin is a fungal antibiotic that inhibits SPTLC2 (Figure 3A) and is commonly used to deplete SM in cells (Courtney et al., 2018; Tafesse et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Myriocin treatment potentiated the response to SHH in NIH/3T3 cells.
claims.source: Myriocin treatment potentiated the response to SHH in NIH/3T3 cells, as measured by the transcriptional induction of Gli1 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Myriocin was sufficient to activate HH signaling in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) even in the absence of added HH ligands.
claims.source: In mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), myriocin was sufficient to activate HH signaling even in the absence of added HH ligands (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Myriocin potentiated the effect of SHH on mouse spinal neural progenitor cells (NPCs), substantially reducing the concentration of SHH required to drive motor neuron differentiation.
claims.source: Mouse spinal neural progenitor cells (NPCs) differentiate into Olig2-expressing motor neuron progenitors in response to moderate concentrations of SHH. Myriocin potentiated the effect of SHH on NPCs, substantially reducing the concentration of SHH required to drive motor neuron differentiation (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Fumonisin B1 amplified HH signaling.
claims.source: First, fumonisin B1, a mycotoxin structurally distinct from myriocin that inhibits a different step in SM synthesis (Figure 3A), also amplified HH signaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The potentiating effect of myriocin on HH signaling could be reversed by the exogenous administration of SM.
claims.source: Second, the potentiating effect of myriocin on HH signaling could be reversed by the exogenous administration of SM (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Increasing SM levels in cells using a low-dose of staurosporine reduced HH signaling strength.
claims.source: Finally, increasing SM levels in cells using a low-dose of staurosporine had the expected opposite effect: reduction of HH signaling strength (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) (Maekawa et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: SM is localized in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.
claims.source: SM is localized in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane (Bretscher, 1972; Murate and Kobayashi, 2016; Verkleij et al., 1973) where it plays key roles in its lateral organization, including the formation of ordered membrane microdomains that can influence protein trafficking, signaling and other processes (Levental and Veatch, 2016; Simons and Ikonen, 2000; Simons and Ikonen, 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: SM plays key roles in the lateral organization of the plasma membrane, including the formation of ordered membrane microdomains.
claims.source: SM is localized in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane (Bretscher, 1972; Murate and Kobayashi, 2016; Verkleij et al., 1973) where it plays key roles in its lateral organization, including the formation of ordered membrane microdomains that can influence protein trafficking, signaling and other processes (Levental and Veatch, 2016; Simons and Ikonen, 2000; Simons and Ikonen, 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Myriocin did not significantly alter the abundances of the HH pathway proteins GLI3, SMO, SUFU or PTCH1.
claims.source: Myriocin did not significantly alter the abundances of the HH pathway proteins GLI3, SMO, SUFU or PTCH1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and also did not change either the frequency or the length of primary cilia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Myriocin did not change either the frequency or the length of primary cilia.
claims.source: Myriocin did not significantly alter the abundances of the HH pathway proteins GLI3, SMO, SUFU or PTCH1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and also did not change either the frequency or the length of primary cilia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: PTCH1 and GPR161 were properly localized in the ciliary membrane in myriocin-treated cells and were cleared from cilia in response to SHH addition.
claims.source: However, both proteins were properly localized in the ciliary membrane in myriocin-treated cells and were cleared (as expected) from cilia in response to SHH addition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: Myriocin potentiated SMO ciliary accumulation in NIH/3T3 cells.
claims.source: The SHH-triggered accumulation of SMO in primary cilia is required for initiation of HH signaling in the cytoplasm (Corbit et al., 2005). Myriocin potentiated SMO ciliary accumulation in NIH/3T3 cells, suggesting that SM depletion enhances SMO activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: HH signaling in cells treated with myriocin was blocked by the SMO antagonist Vismodegib.
claims.source: HH signaling in cells treated with myriocin was blocked by the SMO antagonist Vismodegib (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Myriocin failed to activate HH signaling in Smo-/- cells.
claims.source: Myriocin also failed to activate HH signaling in Smo-/- cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Myriocin acts on SMO, or at a step upstream of SMO.
claims.source: Both observations suggest that myriocin acts on SMO, or at a step upstream of SMO.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results with Vismodegib and Smo-/- cells.

claims.claim: SMO has two potential cholesterol-binding sites: one in the CRD and a second in the TMD.
claims.source: SMO has multiple ligand binding sites: one in the extracellular cysteine-rich domain (CRD) that binds cholesterol and oxysterols and another in the transmembrane domain (TMD) that binds to diverse SMO ligands and to sterols (Byrne et al., 2018; Deshpande et al., 2019; Qi et al., 2019b; Sharpe et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Mutations in the CRD site abolish sterol binding and responses to SHH.
claims.source: Mutations in the CRD site abolish sterol binding and responses to SHH; mutations in the more superficial region of the TMD site prevent SMO activation by synthetic agonists like Smoothened Agonist (SAG) but do not affect responses to SHH (Figure 4B) (Byrne et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Luchetti et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Mutations in the TMD site prevent SMO activation by synthetic agonists like SAG but do not affect responses to SHH.
claims.source: Mutations in the CRD site abolish sterol binding and responses to SHH; mutations in the more superficial region of the TMD site prevent SMO activation by synthetic agonists like Smoothened Agonist (SAG) but do not affect responses to SHH (Figure 4B) (Byrne et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Luchetti et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Mutations in the sterol-binding CRD site (D99A/Y134F) reduced myriocin-driven activation of HH signaling.
claims.source: Previously defined mutations in the sterol-binding CRD site (D99A/Y134F, Figure 4B), which abrogate cholesterol binding by disrupting a key hydrogen bond with the 3β-hydroxyl of cholesterol, reduced myriocin-driven activation (Figure 4C) (Byrne et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: A mutation (D477G) in the TMD site failed to diminish myriocin-induced signaling.
claims.source: In contrast, a mutation (D477G, Figure 4B) in the TMD site failed to diminish myriocin-induced signaling (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: SM regulates SMO activity by controlling the availability of cellular cholesterol that can bind to SMO.
claims.source: The observation that mutations in the CRD of SMO, a well-defined binding site for cholesterol (Byrne et al., 2016), attenuated the effects of SM depletion (Figure 4C) suggested that SM regulates SMO activity by controlling the availability of cellular cholesterol that can bind to SMO.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results with SMO mutants.

claims.claim: Plasma membrane cholesterol is organized in three pools: a fixed pool essential for membrane integrity, a SM-sequestered pool with low chemical activity and a third ('accessible') pool with higher chemical activity.
claims.source: These studies have led to the proposal that plasma membrane cholesterol is organized in three pools: a fixed pool essential for membrane integrity, a SM-sequestered pool with low chemical activity and a third ('accessible') pool with higher chemical activity that is available to interact with proteins and transport to the ER (Das et al., 2014; Lange et al., 2004; Radhakrishnan et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The distribution of cholesterol between the sequestered and accessible pools is determined by the ratio of cholesterol to SM.
claims.source: The distribution of cholesterol between the sequestered and accessible pools is determined by the ratio of cholesterol to SM: SM depletion (or cholesterol addition) leads to an increase in accessible cholesterol (Figure 5A) (Das et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: PFO* binds to the accessible pool of cholesterol.
claims.source: Instead, protein probes derived from lipid-binding toxins have been recently developed to distinguish between the accessible and sequestered pools in intact membranes or cells (Figure 5A): PFO*, derived from the bacterial toxin Perfringolysin O, binds to the accessible pool of cholesterol and OlyA, derived from the fungal toxin Osterolysin A, binds to SM-cholesterol complexes (Das et al., 2013; Endapally et al., 2019a; Flanagan et al., 2009; Skočaj et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: OlyA binds to SM-cholesterol complexes.
claims.source: Instead, protein probes derived from lipid-binding toxins have been recently developed to distinguish between the accessible and sequestered pools in intact membranes or cells (Figure 5A): PFO*, derived from the bacterial toxin Perfringolysin O, binds to the accessible pool of cholesterol and OlyA, derived from the fungal toxin Osterolysin A, binds to SM-cholesterol complexes (Das et al., 2013; Endapally et al., 2019a; Flanagan et al., 2009; Skočaj et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: OlyA_E69A binds to both free SM and SM-cholesterol complexes.
claims.source: A useful point mutant of OlyA (OlyA_E69A) binds to both free SM and SM-cholesterol complexes, allowing measurement of total SM (Figure 5A) (Endapally et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Treatment of cells with myriocin decreased both OlyA and OlyA_E69A staining.
claims.source: Treatment of cells with myriocin decreased both OlyA and OlyA_E69A staining, consistent with SM depletion (Figure 5B and C); staining was restored by the addition of exogenous egg SM (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: Myriocin treatment and cholesterol loading increased PFO* staining.
claims.source: Myriocin treatment and cholesterol loading increased PFO* staining, showing that both treatments increased the level of accessible cholesterol in the plasma membrane (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The depletion of SM with myriocin or other pharmacological agents does not change the abundances of total cellular cholesterol or plasma membrane cholesterol.
claims.source: The depletion of SM with myriocin or other pharmacological agents does not change the abundances of total cellular cholesterol or plasma membrane cholesterol (Das et al., 2014; Tafesse et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Reducing accessible cholesterol in myriocin-treated cells with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) decreased SHH-induced activation of the GLI-GFP reporter.
claims.source: Reducing accessible cholesterol in myriocin-treated cells with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD), measured by PFO* staining, decreased SHH-induced activation of the GLI-GFP reporter (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: SM impairs HH signaling by sequestering cholesterol into complexes where it is inaccessible to SMO.
claims.source: These results, together with the requirement of the cholesterol-binding CRD for the potentiating effect of myriocin (Figure 4C), support the model that SM impairs HH signaling by sequestering cholesterol into complexes where it is inaccessible to SMO.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Purified SMO is constitutively active in nano-discs containing physiological levels of cholesterol in the absence of SM.
claims.source: This conclusion is also consistent with the observation that purified SMO is constitutively active in nano-discs containing physiological levels of cholesterol in the absence of SM (Myers et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: ALOD4 selectively traps accessible cholesterol on the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane without altering cholesterol levels in the cell or plasma membrane.
claims.source: Unlike a reagent like MβCD, which extracts cholesterol from cells, ALOD4 selectively traps accessible cholesterol on the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane without altering cholesterol levels in the cell or plasma membrane (Figure 6A) (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Both ALOD4 and MβCD blocked HH signaling when added to cells.
claims.source: Despite very different mechanisms of action, both ALOD4 and MβCD blocked HH signaling when added to cells (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: ALOD4 induced the expression of Hmgcr.
claims.source: In a control experiment, ALOD4 induced the expression of Hmgcr, the gene encoding the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase, which is known to be induced when accessible cholesterol is depleted (Figure 6C) (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017; Johnson et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: ALOD4 did not change the frequency of ciliation.
claims.source: ALOD4 did not change the frequency of ciliation (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: HH signaling is enhanced by myriocin, which increases accessible cholesterol.
claims.source: In summary, HH signaling is enhanced by myriocin, which increases accessible cholesterol (Figure 5E), but inhibited by ALOD4, which decreases accessible cholesterol.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: HH signaling is inhibited by ALOD4, which decreases accessible cholesterol.
claims.source: In summary, HH signaling is enhanced by myriocin, which increases accessible cholesterol (Figure 5E), but inhibited by ALOD4, which decreases accessible cholesterol.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with ALOD4.

claims.claim: Neither myriocin nor ALOD4 change total cholesterol abundance in cells.
claims.source: Neither myriocin nor ALOD4 change total cholesterol abundance in cells (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017; Tafesse et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Accessible cholesterol is the thermodynamically distinct fraction of total cholesterol that is relevant for the regulation of SMO in HH signaling.
claims.source: We conclude that accessible cholesterol is the thermodynamically distinct fraction of total cholesterol that is relevant for the regulation of SMO in HH signaling.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results with myriocin and ALOD4.

claims.claim: The regulation of SMO by PTCH1 occurs at primary cilia.
claims.source: The regulation of SMO by PTCH1 occurs at primary cilia, the only post-Golgi compartment in the cell where both proteins can be found localized together (Rohatgi et al., 2009; Rohatgi et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The ciliary membrane is thought to have a different lipid and protein composition than the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Since the ciliary membrane is thought to have a different lipid and protein composition than the plasma membrane (Nachury and Mick, 2019), we compared PFO*, OlyA and OlyA_E69A staining in the ciliary membrane relative to the plasma membrane using confocal microscopy.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The ratio of SM to cholesterol is high in the ciliary membrane.
claims.source: In untreated cells, the C/P ratio was significantly higher for OlyA_E69A staining compared to OlyA or PFO* staining (Figure 7A). This suggests that the ratio of SM to cholesterol, which determines the abundance of accessible cholesterol, is high in the ciliary membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the probe staining data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Most cilia of untreated cells did not show distinctive staining for SM-cholesterol complexes (OlyA) or accessible cholesterol (PFO*).
claims.source: Indeed, while OlyA_E69A staining of total SM was readily detectable in cilia, most cilia of untreated cells did not show distinctive staining for SM-cholesterol complexes (OlyA) or accessible cholesterol (PFO*) (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Cholesterol loading increased the C/P ratio of SM-cholesterol complexes (OlyA staining).
claims.source: Cholesterol loading increased the C/P ratio of SM-cholesterol complexes (OlyA staining, Figure 7B and D), showing that a significant proportion of SM molecules at cilia are free to pair with exogenously added cholesterol.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claims.claim: Myriocin treatment increased the amount of accessible cholesterol in the ciliary membrane relative to the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Myriocin treatment, which reduced SM levels in both the plasma membrane and the ciliary membrane (Figure 5B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), increased the amount of accessible cholesterol in the ciliary membrane relative to the plasma membrane (PFO* staining, Figure 7C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claims.claim: SM provides the major restraint on cholesterol accessibility at cilia.
claims.source: Indeed, myriocin had a greater effect on the C/P ratio of accessible cholesterol compared to even cholesterol loading, suggesting that SM provides the major restraint on cholesterol accessibility at cilia (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The ciliary membrane is significantly more resistant (compared to the plasma membrane) to permeabilization by both PFO and cholesterol-binding detergents like digitonin.
claims.source: A high ratio of SM to cholesterol provides a potential explanation for the observation that the ciliary membrane is significantly more resistant (compared to the plasma membrane) to permeabilization by both PFO and cholesterol-binding detergents like digitonin (Breslow et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: SHH did not induce much of a change in PFO* staining of the bulk plasma membrane.
claims.source: SHH did not induce much of a change in PFO* staining of the bulk plasma membrane, measured by flow cytometry (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: SHH led to a rapid increase in accessible cholesterol in the ciliary membrane when cells were treated with myriocin or loaded with cholesterol.
claims.source: In contrast, SHH led to a rapid increase in accessible cholesterol in the ciliary membrane, either when cells were treated with myriocin or when cells were loaded with cholesterol (Figure 8B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claims.claim: SHH did not change ciliary PFO* staining in Ptch1-/- cells.
claims.source: SHH did not change ciliary PFO* staining in Ptch1-/- cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Activation of signaling with SAG did not cause significant changes in accessible cholesterol at the ciliary membrane.
claims.source: In addition, activation of signaling with SAG, which bypasses PTCH1 and directly activates SMO, also did not cause significant changes in accessible cholesterol at the ciliary membrane (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The SHH-induced change in accessible cholesterol at primary cilia is dependent on PTCH1 activity.
claims.source: Both controls show that the SHH-induced change in accessible cholesterol at primary cilia is dependent on PTCH1 activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results with Ptch1-/- cells and SAG treatment.

claims.claim: Only a fraction of total plasma membrane cholesterol is relevant to the regulation of HH signaling.
claims.source: First, only a fraction of total plasma membrane cholesterol is relevant to the regulation of HH signaling. This thermodynamically distinct pool of accessible cholesterol with high chemical activity ranges from ~2% of total plasma membrane cholesterol in lipid depleted cells to ~15% of total plasma membrane cholesterol in lipid replete cells (Das et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The changes in accessible cholesterol that regulate SMO are confined to a subcellular compartment, the primary cilium.
claims.source: Second, the changes in accessible cholesterol that regulate SMO are confined to a subcellular compartment, the primary cilium, where PTCH1, SMO and the cytoplasmic signaling machinery downstream of SMO are localized.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing compartmentalized changes in accessible cholesterol.

claims.claim: The lipid composition of primary cilia may be dynamically altered to control the activity or trafficking of cilia-localized proteins.
claims.source: Phosphoinositides and oxysterols are examples of other lipids whose abundances in the ciliary membrane are different from the plasma membrane (Chávez et al., 2015; Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2015; Raleigh et al., 2018), supporting the general principle that the lipid composition of primary cilia may be dynamically altered to control the activity or trafficking of cilia-localized proteins (Nachury and Mick, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and inference from the current findings.

claims.claim: SCAP senses accessible cholesterol in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to regulate the transcription of genes that control cholesterol biosynthesis.
claims.source: Another pathway that detects and responds to accessible cholesterol is the SCAP/SREBP signaling system, which provided an important precedent (and inspiration) for our work (Brown et al., 2018; Brown and Goldstein, 2009). SCAP senses accessible cholesterol in a specific subcellular compartment, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), to regulate the transcription of genes that control cholesterol biosynthesis (Radhakrishnan et al., 2008; Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Continual transport of cholesterol from the plasma membrane to the ER ensures that information about changes in plasma membrane cholesterol accessibility is transmitted to the ER, where SCAP is localized.
claims.source: Continual transport of cholesterol from the plasma membrane to the ER ensures that information about changes in plasma membrane cholesterol accessibility is transmitted to the ER, where SCAP is localized (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: PTCH1 may selectively transport the pool of accessible cholesterol to a yet unknown membrane or protein acceptor.
claims.source: We suggest that PTCH1 may selectively transport the pool of accessible cholesterol (rather than the fixed or SM-bound pool) to a yet unknown membrane or protein acceptor (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Selective transport of accessible cholesterol has been previously proposed for other cholesterol transporter proteins.
claims.source: Selective transport of accessible cholesterol has been previously proposed for other cholesterol transporter proteins (Lange and Steck, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: PTCH1 could transport cholesterol from the ciliary membrane to a sterol transport protein or a membrane compartment in the cytoplasm.
claims.source: The direction of sterol transfer by PTCH1 remains uncertain: it could transport cholesterol in the same direction as its relative NPC1 (from the ciliary membrane to a sterol transport protein or a membrane compartment in the cytoplasm) or in an outward direction from the ciliary membrane to an extracellular acceptor (see arrows labeled 1 and 2 in Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative and presents alternative hypotheses.

claims.claim: PTCH1 could transport cholesterol in an outward direction from the ciliary membrane to an extracellular acceptor.

claims.claim: The 'pump-leak' model may be energetically sustainable because PTCH1 is tasked with reducing accessible cholesterol only over the small surface area of the ciliary membrane.
claims.source: This 'pump-leak' model may be energetically sustainable because PTCH1 is tasked with reducing accessible cholesterol only over the small surface area of the ciliary membrane (~400 fold smaller than that of the plasma membrane) (Nachury, 2014).

results.result: A focused CRISPR screen targeting 1244 lipid-related genes identified cholesterol biosynthesis pathway genes as positive regulators and sphingolipid biosynthesis pathway genes as negative regulators of HH signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C27 describe the CRISPR screen design, validation with positive controls (C19-C20), and identification of two major lipid pathways affecting HH signaling (C26-C27). The screen correctly identified known regulators and revealed statistically significant clustering in cholesterol and sphingolipid pathways, supported by Figure 1B-D.

results.result: Cholesterol biosynthesis genes are required for HH signaling, and cholesterol itself (rather than precursors or metabolites like 24(S),25-epoxycholesterol) is the endogenous sterol regulating SMO activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C38 demonstrate that CRISPR knockout of cholesterol biosynthesis genes (Lss, Dhcr7, Dhcr24) impairs HH signaling, with rescue by exogenous cholesterol in Lss-/- and Dhcr7-/- but not Dhcr24-/- cells. The Dhcr24 result (C40-C41) provides genetic evidence against 24(S),25-epoxycholesterol as the key regulator, supporting cholesterol itself (C42). Mass spectrometry data (C34-C35) confirm expected sterol changes.

results.result: Sphingomyelin (SM) negatively regulates HH signaling, as demonstrated by pharmacological depletion with myriocin or fumonisin B1 potentiating HH responses, with effects reversed by SM addition and opposite effects with SM elevation.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 provide convergent pharmacological evidence: myriocin (SM depletion) potentiates HH signaling in multiple cell types (NIH/3T3, MEFs, NPCs), fumonisin B1 (different mechanism, same outcome) shows similar effects (C51), SM add-back reverses myriocin effects (C52), and staurosporine (increases SM) reduces signaling (C53). The identification of Sgms1 in the screen (C45) supports SM as the relevant sphingolipid.

results.result: Myriocin-induced potentiation of HH signaling acts at the level of SMO or upstream, without affecting ciliary structure, protein abundances, or trafficking of negative regulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 demonstrate myriocin does not affect HH pathway protein levels, ciliation frequency/length, or PTCH1/GPR161 localization. Claims C60-C62 show myriocin effects require SMO (blocked by Vismodegib, absent in Smo-/- cells), localizing the effect to SMO or upstream. Enhanced SMO ciliary accumulation (C59) supports SMO activation.

results.result: SM regulates SMO activity through the cholesterol-binding CRD site, as mutations in the CRD (D99A/Y134F) but not the TMD site (D477G) reduce myriocin-driven HH activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 provide critical mutagenesis data showing CRD mutations (which abolish cholesterol binding, C64) reduce myriocin effects while TMD mutations (which affect SAG binding, C65) do not. This supports the inference (C68) that SM regulates SMO by controlling cholesterol availability to the CRD. The structural context (C63) and prior characterization (C64-C65) provide necessary background.

results.result: SM sequesters cholesterol into complexes with low chemical activity, and SM depletion increases accessible cholesterol without changing total cholesterol, thereby enhancing HH signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 establish the three-pool model of membrane cholesterol from prior work. Claims C71-C75 demonstrate that toxin-based probes (PFO*, OlyA, OlyA_E69A) can distinguish these pools and show myriocin increases accessible cholesterol (PFO* staining) while depleting SM. Claim C76 confirms total cholesterol is unchanged. The rescue experiment (C77) showing MβCD reverses myriocin effects supports the model (C78) that SM sequesters cholesterol from SMO.

results.result: Accessible cholesterol, not total cholesterol, regulates HH signaling, as demonstrated by ALOD4 (which traps accessible cholesterol without removing it) blocking HH signaling similarly to MβCD.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 establish ALOD4 as an orthogonal tool that traps accessible cholesterol without changing total levels, confirmed by Hmgcr induction (C82) and no effect on ciliation (C83). Claims C84-C86 show opposite effects of myriocin (increases accessible cholesterol, enhances signaling) and ALOD4 (decreases accessible cholesterol, blocks signaling), both without changing total cholesterol. This strongly supports C87 that accessible cholesterol is the regulatory pool.

results.result: The ciliary membrane has a high SM:cholesterol ratio resulting in low accessible cholesterol, with SM providing the major restraint on cholesterol accessibility at cilia.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 show that untreated cilia have high total SM (OlyA_E69A) but low SM-cholesterol complexes (OlyA) and accessible cholesterol (PFO*), indicating high SM:cholesterol ratio. Claims C92-C93 demonstrate cholesterol loading and myriocin treatment increase ciliary accessible cholesterol. Claim C94 shows myriocin has greater effects than cholesterol loading, supporting SM as the major restraint. The resistance to permeabilization (C95) provides independent support for this lipid organization.

results.result: SHH ligands increase accessible cholesterol specifically in the ciliary membrane (not bulk plasma membrane) in a PTCH1-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 shows SHH does not significantly affect bulk plasma membrane accessible cholesterol. Claim C97 demonstrates SHH rapidly increases ciliary accessible cholesterol in myriocin-treated or cholesterol-loaded cells. Controls with Ptch1-/- cells (C98) and SAG treatment (C99) show this effect requires PTCH1 activity (C100), supporting the model that PTCH1 inactivation by SHH increases ciliary accessible cholesterol.

results.result: Accessible cholesterol regulation of SMO is confined to the primary cilium, where only 2-15% of total membrane cholesterol is accessible and changes are compartmentalized.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 synthesize the key findings that only a small fraction of cholesterol is accessible (citing prior work) and that regulatory changes are confined to the cilium where PTCH1 and SMO colocalize. Claim C103 places this in broader context of dynamic ciliary lipid regulation. These claims are well-supported by the compartmentalized changes shown in C96-C97.

results.result: A proposed 'pump-leak' model suggests PTCH1 selectively transports accessible cholesterol from the ciliary membrane, with SM levels setting the threshold for SMO activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C114 present a speculative mechanistic model for how PTCH1 might regulate ciliary accessible cholesterol. While the model is consistent with the data (C115-C116 provide supporting observations), key aspects remain untested: the direction of cholesterol transport (C108-C109), the identity of acceptors (C106), and the energetics of the pump-leak system (C111-C112). The model is plausible but requires direct demonstration of PTCH1 transport activity.

results.result: SM is localized in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane where it plays key roles in membrane organization including formation of ordered microdomains.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 describe established properties of SM from prior work (multiple citations), providing necessary background for understanding SM's role in cholesterol sequestration. This is well-established knowledge appropriately cited.

results.result: SM depletion affects cholesterol accessibility in both membrane leaflets due to rapid cholesterol flip-flop, potentially impacting both CRD and TMD cholesterol-binding sites on SMO.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124 explain how SM (outer leaflet only) depletion affects both leaflets through cholesterol flip-flop, supported by citations. Claims C118-C121 describe the two cholesterol-binding sites on SMO and their potential regulation. This discussion appropriately acknowledges that the experiments cannot distinguish which leaflet/site is more important, showing appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The lack of cholesterol biosynthesis regulation in Drosophila may explain why HH signaling is not confined to primary cilia in insects.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 accurately describe differences between Drosophila and vertebrate cholesterol biology (supported by citations). However, C129 is highly speculative, proposing an evolutionary explanation without direct evidence. While intellectually interesting, this hypothesis would require comparative functional studies to test.

results.result: Prior work established that cholesterol binds and activates SMO, and proposed that PTCH1 regulates SMO by restricting cholesterol access, though PTCH1 transport activity remains undemonstrated in purified systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C11 accurately cite prior work establishing cholesterol-SMO interaction and PTCH1's structural similarity to cholesterol transporters. Claims C12-C13 appropriately note limitations of existing evidence (resolution of structures, lack of direct transport demonstration), providing context for the current study.

results.result: Cholesterol is highly abundant (up to 50% of plasma membrane lipids), and other lipids including oxysterols can also regulate SMO activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 provide background on cholesterol abundance and alternative SMO-regulating lipids, appropriately cited to prior work. This contextualizes the challenge of how an abundant lipid can serve as a specific regulator.

results.result: Accessible cholesterol in the ciliary membrane drives SMO activation and HH signaling, regulated by sphingomyelin sequestration and PTCH1-mediated changes in response to HH ligands.
results.evaluation: These abstract claims (C2-C7) summarize the main findings of the paper. They are well-supported by the detailed experimental results grouped in other result categories. This represents an accurate high-level summary of the work's major conclusions.
